description: Take the Brandenburg Gate apart piece by piece in 3D, and read the story of the gate: from Prussian peace monument to Napoleon's trophy, from war ruin to the symbol of reunified Germany.
intro: Berlin's most famous landmark is 26 meters of sandstone that has watched Prussian kings, Napoleon's army, Nazi rallies, and the fall of the Berlin Wall. This is how a city gate became the symbol of a reunited country.

sections.alt: The Quadriga on top of the Brandenburg Gate
sections.body: Commissioned by Frederick William II of Prussia and designed by Carl Gotthard Langhans, the gate was built between 1788 and 1791, modeled on the Propylaea of ancient Athens. Twelve Doric columns form five passageways through a structure 26 meters high and over 60 meters wide. It was first called the Friedenstor, the Peace Gate. In 1793 Johann Gottfried Schadow crowned it with the Quadriga: four horses pulling a chariot driven by the goddess of peace, the first quadriga built since antiquity.
sections.caption: The Quadriga, sculpted by Johann Gottfried Schadow and installed in 1793.
sections.credit: Yair Haklai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: A gate for peace

sections.body: After Prussia's defeat at Jena-Auerstedt in 1806, Napoleon marched through the gate and carried the Quadriga off to Paris as a war trophy. When Napoleon fell, Prussian troops brought it home in 1814. The architect Karl Friedrich Schinkel reworked it for the occasion: the goddess of peace became Victoria, goddess of victory, and she was given an Iron Cross crowned with the Prussian eagle.
sections.heading: Stolen, returned, rebranded

sections.alt: The Brandenburg Gate in ruins in May 1945 with a Soviet victory banner
sections.body: The Nazis adopted the gate as a party symbol and placed it on the axis of their planned world capital Germania. The war left it bullet-scarred; the Quadriga was destroyed, and only a single horse's head survived, now kept in the Markisches Museum. When Soviet troops took Berlin in 1945, they raised the red banner of victory on the ruined Quadriga.
sections.caption: The gate in May 1945, with a Soviet victory banner on the ruined Quadriga.
sections.credit: Alexey Shapochkin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: Scarred by war

sections.alt: Crowds at the reopened border crossing at the Brandenburg Gate in December 1989
sections.body: When the Berlin Wall went up on 13 August 1961, it ran directly past the gate's western side. The gate stood in the death strip, unreachable from East and West alike, for 28 years. It was there, with the gate behind him, that Ronald Reagan demanded on 12 June 1987: Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
sections.caption: The border crossing at the gate the day after it reopened, 23 December 1989.
sections.credit: Bundesarchiv, Bild 183-1989-1223-300 / CC-BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sections.heading: Twenty-eight years behind the Wall

sections.body: On 9 November 1989 the Wall fell and thousands celebrated at the gate. On 22 December 1989 the crossing reopened, with Helmut Kohl walking through to meet Hans Modrow before a crowd of 100,000. The Quadriga was restored, the Iron Cross returned, and the gate itself was refurbished from 2000 to 2002. Today it is the symbol of reunified Germany: the finish line of the Berlin Marathon, the stage for New Year's Eve, and the first thing the world pictures when it thinks of Berlin.
